'''Henry Howland Crapo''' ({{respell|KRAY|poh}};<ref>{{cite web|url=https://mathoverflow.net/questions/4394/pronunciation-crapo|title=Pronunciation: Crapo|website=MathOverflow|access-date=October 25, 2019}}</ref> August 12, 1932 – September 3, 2019) was an American-Canadian mathematician who worked in [[algebraic combinatorics]]. Over the course of his career, he held positions at several universities and research institutes in Canada and France.  He is noted for his work in [[matroid theory]] and [[lattice theory]].

==Education and career==
Crapo was born in [[Detroit]], [[Michigan]], in 1932.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://uwaterloo.ca/pure-mathematics/news/remembering-henry-crapo|title=Remembering Henry Crapo|website=uwaterloo.ca|date=October 25, 2019 |publisher=[[University of Waterloo]]|access-date=October 31, 2019}}</ref><ref name="ensordonation">{{cite web|url=https://www.kmska.be/en/collection/maths-genius-donates-james-ensor-painting
|title=Maths Genius Donates James Ensor Painting|website=Collection|publisher=Royal Museum of Fine Arts Antwerp|access-date=October 25, 2019}}</ref> He received his Ph.D. in 1964 under the supervision of [[Gian-Carlo Rota]] and Kenneth Hoffman, with thesis ''On the theory of combinatorial independence''.<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=13377|title=Henry Howland Crapo}}</ref><ref name="thesis">{{cite thesis|first=Henry H.|last=Crapo|title=On the theory of combinatorial independence|year=1964|publisher=[[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]]|hdl=1721.1/138650 | url=https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/138650}}</ref> While working on his thesis, he was an assistant professor at [[Northeastern University]] in [[Boston]].<ref name="thesis"/><ref>{{citation|first=Henry H.|last=Crapo|title=Single-element extensions of matroids|journal= Journal of Research of the National Bureau of Standards Section B |volume= 69B |issue=1–2 |year=1965|pages=55–65|doi=10.6028/jres.069B.003 |mr=0190045|url=https://archive.org/details/jresv69Bn1-2p55}}</ref> He subsequently held academic positions at the [[University of Waterloo]], [[Université de Montréal]], [[French Institute for Research in Computer Science and Automation|INRIA]] Rocquencourt, and [[École des Hautes Études en Sciences Sociales]].<ref name="advissue">{{cite journal | last=Kung | first=Joseph P.S. | title=Guest Editor's Introduction | journal=[[Advances in Applied Mathematics]] | volume=23 | issue=1 | year=1999 | doi=10.1006/aama.1999.0642 | pages=1–2| doi-access=free }}</ref> During his time in Waterloo, Crapo became a Canadian citizen.<ref name="ensordonation"/>

Crapo is known for his early work in [[matroid]] theory, and for related work in lattice theory. He introduced the [[Matroid#Beta invariant|beta invariant]] of a matroid,<ref>{{cite journal | last=Crapo | first=Henry H. | title=A higher invariant for matroids | journal=[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory]] | volume=2 | issue=4 | year=1967 | doi=10.1016/s0021-9800(67)80051-6 | pages=406–417 | mr=0215744| doi-access=free }}</ref> and published the first paper on the [[Tutte polynomial]]<ref>{{cite journal | last=Crapo | first=Henry H. | title=The Tutte polynomial | journal=Aequationes Mathematicae | volume=3 | issue=3 | year=1969 | doi=10.1007/bf01817442 | pages=211–229|mr=0215744| s2cid=119602825 }}</ref> (though Tutte had already defined an equivalent polynomial in his thesis). Together with Gian-Carlo Rota, Crapo wrote the first book on matroid theory.<ref>{{cite book | last1=Crapo | first1=Henry | last2=Rota | first2=Gian-Carlo | author2-link=Gian-Carlo Rota | title=On the Foundations of Combinatorial Theory: Combinatorial Geometries | publisher=[[M.I.T. Press]] | location=Cambridge, Massachusetts | year=1970 | isbn=978-0-262-53016-3 | oclc=117282 | mr=0290980 | url-access=registration | url=https://archive.org/details/onfoundationsofc00crap }}</ref><ref name="matroidunionobit">{{cite web|url=http://matroidunion.org/?p=2443|title= Henry Crapo: A Brief Reminiscence |author-last=Oxley|author-first=James|author-link=James Oxley|website=Matroid Union|date= October 21, 2019 }}</ref>  He is also known for Crapo's Complementation Theorem in [[Möbius inversion formula#On posets|poset Möbius Inversion]].<ref>{{cite journal | last=Crapo | first=Henry H. | title=The Möbius function of a lattice | journal=Journal of Combinatorial Theory | volume=1 | issue=1 | year=1966 | doi=10.1016/s0021-9800(66)80009-1 | pages=126–131 | mr=0193018| doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite book | last=Stanley | first=Richard | author-link=Richard P. Stanley |title=Enumerative combinatorics | publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] | location=New York | year=2012 | isbn=978-1-107-60262-5 | oclc=777400915 |mr=2868112}}</ref>  Crapo wrote 65 mathematical publications during his career.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/search/author.html?mrauthid=213847 |title=Henry H. Crapo author profile|website=[[MathSciNet]]|publisher=American Mathematical Society|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

Upon his retirement, Crapo moved to the south of [[France]].<ref name="ensordonation"/> He continued some mathematical activity, and hosted several small conferences at his house there.<ref name="matroidunionobit"/> He died on September 3, 2019.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://carnet.midilibre.fr/deces/henry-crapo/55735861|title=Henry Crapo Death Notice|language=fr|access-date=October 25, 2019 }}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
* A special 1999 issue of the journal ''[[Advances in Applied Mathematics]]'' was dedicated to Crapo on the occasion of his 67th birthday.<ref name="advissue"/><ref>{{cite journal | last=Penne | first=Rudi | title=Almost Flat Line Configurations | journal=Advances in Applied Mathematics | volume=23 | issue=1 | year=1999 | doi=10.1006/aama.1999.0647 | pages=54–77 | mr=1692976| doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Personal life==
[[File:UWaterloo Porcellino.jpg |thumb|alt=a large bronze statue of boar|The University of Waterloo [[Porcellino]], donated by Crapo|upright=0.75]]
Crapo was a patron of the arts.  At the [[University of Waterloo]] he donated a collection of rare books on the history of dance and ballet,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://uwaterloo.ca/library/special-collections-archives/collections/crapo-henry-h|title=Crapo, Henry H.|website=Special Collections & Archives|date=July 17, 2014|publisher=University of Waterloo Library|access-date=October 25, 2019|archive-date=October 23, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191023195427/https://uwaterloo.ca/library/special-collections-archives/collections/crapo-henry-h|url-status=dead}}</ref> as well as a copy of the [[Porcellino]] sculpture of Florence; the latter shoulder-high bronze sculpture of a wild boar later became a mascot for the [[University of Waterloo Faculty of Arts]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://uwaterloo.ca/library/special-collections-archives/exhibits/celebrating-boar/boar-news|title=The Boar in the News|website=Special Collections & Archives|date=March 6, 2015 |publisher=University of Waterloo Library|access-date=October 25, 2019}}</ref> He also donated ''The Temptation of St. Anthony'' by [[James Ensor]] to the [[Royal Museum of Fine Arts Antwerp|Royal Museum of Fine Arts in Antwerp]]<ref name="ensordonation"/> and ''Corpse of Man'' by [[Hyman Bloom]] to the [[Rose Art Museum]] at [[Brandeis University]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://rosecollection.brandeis.edu/objects-1/info/1837|title=Corpse of Man|publisher=[[Rose Art Museum]]|website=rosecollection.brandeis.edu|access-date=March 27, 2024}}</ref>
